los.text: Describe how ear anatomy relates to pathology. Describe how to perform hearing tests and interpret results.
sessions: Introduction to ENT: Ear Anatomy, Hearing and hearing tests
los.html:
Ear anatomy → pathology
  • External ear (auricle, EAM: lateral ⅓ cartilage with hairs/cerumen glands, medial ⅔ bone): otitis externa, wax impaction, foreign bodies, exostoses (cold-water swimmers), perichondritis/haematoma (auricle: "cauliflower ear"), necrotising otitis externa (elderly diabetics: skull base osteomyelitis).
  • Tympanic membrane/middle ear (ossicles, Eustachian tube, mastoid air cells, facial nerve, chorda tympani): acute otitis media, otitis media with effusion (glue ear), perforation, cholesteatoma, otosclerosis (stapes fixation), mastoiditis, facial palsy.
  • Inner ear (cochlea, vestibule, semicircular canals, CN VIII): presbycusis, noise-induced loss (4 kHz notch), ototoxicity (aminoglycosides, cisplatin, loop diuretics), Ménière's, BPPV, vestibular neuritis/labyrinthitis, vestibular schwannoma, sudden SNHL.
Conductive (external/middle ear: sound transmission) vs sensorineural (cochlea/nerve) hearing loss.
Tuning fork tests (512 Hz)
  • Rinne: fork on mastoid (bone conduction, BC) then beside ear (air conduction, AC). Normal/positive: AC > BC. Negative (BC > AC) = conductive loss in that ear. SNHL: AC > BC (both reduced).
  • Weber: fork on forehead/vertex. Normal: central. Lateralises to the affected ear in conductive loss; to the better (unaffected) ear in sensorineural loss.
Audiometry
  • Pure-tone audiogram (thresholds 250–8000 Hz; air–bone gap = conductive; both lines down = SNHL; normal ≤20 dB HL)
  • Tympanometry (middle ear compliance: type A normal, type B flat = effusion/perforation, type C negative pressure = Eustachian tube dysfunction)
  • Speech audiometry
  • Otoacoustic emissions (newborn screening)
  • ABR (auditory brainstem response).
Whisper test as bedside screen.

los.text: Describe how to diagnose and manage patients presenting with hearing loss, tinnitus, ear discharge, ear pain or vertigo.
los.html:
Hearing loss
  • Conductive: wax (remove: drops, microsuction), otitis externa, OME (children: watchful waiting 3 months → grommets/hearing aids), AOM, perforation (most heal; myringoplasty), cholesteatoma (foul discharge, conductive loss; surgery), otosclerosis (FHx, young women, pregnancy worsens; hearing aid or stapedectomy).
  • Sensorineural: presbycusis (bilateral, high frequency; hearing aids), noise, ototoxic drugs, Ménière's, sudden SNHL (emergency: urgent ENT within 24 h, oral high-dose steroids), unilateral/asymmetric SNHL → MRI internal acoustic meatus (vestibular schwannoma); cochlear implants for severe–profound loss.
Tinnitus
  • Perception of sound without external source
  • Mostly associated with hearing loss.
  • Red flags: unilateral (MRI IAM), pulsatile (vascular: AV malformation, glomus tumour, IIH → imaging), with neurological signs, sudden hearing loss, distress/suicidality.
  • Mx: treat cause, hearing aids, sound therapy, CBT, tinnitus retraining.
Ear discharge (otorrhoea)
  • Otitis externa (itchy, painful, debris; topical antibiotic/steroid drops (e.g. ciprofloxacin, Otomize), aural toilet, wick if swollen)
  • AOM with perforation (mucopurulent)
  • Chronic suppurative otitis media
  • Cholesteatoma (persistent foul-smelling discharge)
  • CSF otorrhoea (trauma).
  • Diabetic elderly with severe pain + granulation tissue → necrotising otitis externa (IV antibiotics, CT/MRI).
Ear pain (otalgia)
  • AOM (children; viral/S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae: most resolve; amoxicillin if systemically unwell, <2 yrs bilateral, otorrhoea, or no improvement at 3 days)
  • Otitis externa (tragal pain)
  • Furunculosis
  • Perichondritis
  • Mastoiditis (post-auricular swelling, protruding ear: IV antibiotics, CT, surgery)
  • Herpes zoster oticus (Ramsay Hunt: vesicles + facial palsy).
  • Referred otalgia (normal ear exam): dental
  • TMJ dysfunction
  • Tonsillitis/quinsy
  • Pharyngeal/laryngeal cancer (via IX/X: "persistent unexplained otalgia in smoker → look in throat")
  • Cervical spine.
VertigoSee LO 3.

los.text: Describe how to diagnose and manage patients presenting with vertigo.
sessions: Physiology of balance and 4 main ENT causes of imbalance
los.html:
VertigoIllusion of movement (spinning) from vestibular system dysfunction; distinguish from presyncope (light-headed), disequilibrium (unsteady), non-specific dizziness.
Key historyTiming and duration of attacks, triggers (head movement, standing), associated hearing loss/tinnitus/aural fullness, neurological symptoms (diplopia, dysarthria, weakness: central), headache, trauma, drugs.
CauseDurationFeaturesDiagnosis / management
BPPV (commonest)Seconds (<1 min)Triggered by head movement (rolling in bed, looking up); otoconia in posterior semicircular canalDix–Hallpike (torsional upbeating nystagmus after latency, fatigable) → Epley manoeuvre (repositioning); Brandt–Daroff exercises
Vestibular neuritis / labyrinthitisDays (single episode)Sudden severe constant vertigo, nausea/vomiting, often post-viral; labyrinthitis also has hearing lossHead impulse test abnormal (corrective saccade), unidirectional horizontal nystagmus; short course vestibular sedatives (prochlorperazine ≤3 days), vestibular rehabilitation
Ménière's diseaseMinutes to hours (20 min–12 h)Episodic vertigo + fluctuating low-frequency SNHL + tinnitus + aural fullness; endolymphatic hydropsAudiogram; low-salt diet, betahistine (limited evidence), intratympanic steroids/gentamicin; DVLA notification
Vestibular migraineMinutes to daysMigraine history, photophobiaMigraine prophylaxis
Central causesVariablePosterior circulation stroke/TIA, MS, cerebellar tumour, vestibular schwannoma (slowly progressive, unilateral hearing loss)HINTS exam (Head Impulse normal, Nystagmus direction-changing/vertical, Test of Skew positive → central), urgent MRI
  • Examination: ENT exam (otoscopy), cranial nerves, cerebellar signs, gait/Romberg, nystagmus, head impulse test, Dix–Hallpike, BP lying/standing, hearing (tuning forks, audiogram).

los.text: Describe how ENT conditions will present differently in the Paediatric population and how they are managed.
los.html:
• Children differ: narrower
    • shorter
    • more horizontal Eustachian tube (more middle ear disease)
    • relatively large tonsils and adenoids (peak 3–7 yrs)
    • narrow airways (small swelling → big obstruction: Poiseuille)
    • immature immunity
    • can't describe symptoms (irritability, ear-pulling, poor feeding, speech delay)
    • developmental impact of hearing loss.
ConditionPresentationManagement
Acute otitis mediaFever, otalgia, irritability, bulging red TM, ± perforation/dischargeAnalgesia; most resolve in 3 days; amoxicillin if criteria (see LO 2); complications: mastoiditis, facial palsy, meningitis
Otitis media with effusion (glue ear)Hearing loss, speech/language delay, behavioural/school problems; dull retracted TM, fluid level; Down syndrome, cleft palate ↑ riskAudiometry/tympanometry (type B); watchful waiting 3 months; grommets (ventilation tubes) ± adenoidectomy, or hearing aids
Recurrent tonsillitisSore throat, fever, exudatePenicillin V; tonsillectomy if ≥7 episodes/1 yr, ≥5/yr for 2 yrs, or ≥3/yr for 3 yrs (SIGN criteria)
Adenotonsillar hypertrophy / paediatric OSASnoring, apnoeas, mouth breathing, restless sleep, daytime behavioural problems/ADHD-like, enuresis, faltering growthSleep study; adenotonsillectomy
Foreign bodies (ear, nose: unilateral foul discharge; button batteries emergency)Removal; button battery in nose/oesophagus = emergency
  • Airway: croup (stridor, barking cough: dexamethasone)
  • Epiglottitis (drooling, toxic, tripod: don't examine throat, anaesthetic/ENT airway)
  • Laryngomalacia (inspiratory stridor in infants, usually resolves)
  • Subglottic stenosis
Congenital hearing lossNewborn hearing screening (OAE/ABR)Hearing aids, cochlear implants early (language development)
Neck lumps: reactive lymphadenopathy (commonest), thyroglossal cyst (moves with tongue protrusion), branchial cyst, dermoid
Periorbital/orbital cellulitis (ethmoid sinusitis)Eyelid swelling; red flags: proptosis, ↓ vision, painful eye movementsIV antibiotics, CT, ENT/ophthalmology

los.text: Identify the pharyngeal arches, pouches and clefts, and recall the major derivatives of each
los.html:
• Pharyngeal (branchial) apparatus (weeks 4–5): 6 arches (5th rudimentary)
    • each arch has mesoderm/neural crest core with artery, nerve, cartilage, muscle
    • between them externally clefts (ectoderm) and internally pouches (endoderm).
ArchNerveMusclesSkeletalArtery
1st (mandibular)V3 (mandibular)Muscles of mastication, mylohyoid, anterior digastric, tensor tympani, tensor veli palatiniMeckel's cartilage: malleus, incus, sphenomandibular ligament; (mandible, maxilla by membranous ossification)Maxillary artery (part)
2nd (hyoid)VII (facial)Muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, posterior digastricReichert's cartilage: stapes, styloid process, stylohyoid ligament, lesser horn + upper body of hyoidStapedial artery (regresses)
3rdIX (glossopharyngeal)StylopharyngeusGreater horn + lower body of hyoidCommon and internal carotid
4thX (superior laryngeal)Cricothyroid, pharyngeal constrictors, levator veli palatiniThyroid, cricoid cartilages (4th + 6th)Aortic arch (left), right subclavian
6thX (recurrent laryngeal)Intrinsic laryngeal muscles (except cricothyroid)Arytenoid, corniculate, cuneiform cartilagesPulmonary arteries, ductus arteriosus
PouchDerivative
1stMiddle ear cavity, Eustachian tube, mastoid antrum
2ndPalatine tonsil (crypts)
3rdInferior parathyroids (dorsal) + thymus (ventral)
4thSuperior parathyroids + ultimobranchial body (→ C cells of thyroid)
Clefts
  • 1st cleft → external acoustic meatus
  • 2nd–4th clefts are overgrown by 2nd arch (cervical sinus) → normally obliterated
  • Persistence → branchial cyst/sinus/fistula (anterior border of SCM).
Membranes1st → tympanic membrane.
Anomalies
  • DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion: 3rd/4th pouch failure → hypoparathyroidism (hypocalcaemia), thymic aplasia (T-cell deficiency), cardiac outflow defects, cleft palate, facial features: "CATCH-22")
  • Treacher Collins (1st arch: mandibular hypoplasia)
  • Pierre Robin sequence
  • Branchial cysts
  • First arch syndromes.

los.text: Describe how nasal anatomy relates to pathology. Describe the normal function of the nose. Describe the examination of the nose
los.html:
StructureLinked pathology
SeptumDeviation → obstruction; septal haematoma after trauma → drain urgently or risk perforation/saddle nose
Little's areaAnterior epistaxis
TurbinatesHypertrophy in rhinitis
Ostiomeatal complexBlockage → sinusitis
Cribriform plate / olfactory cleftCSF leak and anosmia after trauma; anosmia from polyps
Orbit (lamina papyracea)Orbital cellulitis
Cranial cavityFrontal sinusitis → intracranial abscess, meningitis; danger-triangle veins → cavernous sinus thrombosis
Adenoids (children)Nasal obstruction
Normal function
  • Airway (~50% of total airway resistance)
  • Filtering (vibrissae, mucus)
  • Warming and humidifying inspired air (turbinates, rich vascular plexus)
  • Mucociliary clearance (towards nasopharynx)
  • Olfaction (and flavour)
  • Immune defence (IgA, lysozyme)
  • Voice resonance
  • Nasal cycle
  • Reflexes (sneeze)
  • Drainage of sinuses and tears.
Examination of the nose
  • External inspection (front, sides, from above/below): deformity, deviation, swelling, skin lesions, scars, saddle nose.
  • Palpation: nasal bones (crepitus, tenderness), sinuses (tenderness).
  • Airway patency: cold metal spatula/mirror misting test, or occlude each nostril in turn and sniff.
  • Anterior rhinoscopy: tilt nose tip up (Thudichum speculum or otoscope with large speculum, headlight): inspect vestibule, septum (deviation, perforation, haematoma, Little's area vessels), inferior turbinates (size, colour: pale/boggy in allergy), polyps (pale grey, insensate, mobile vs turbinates which are pink/sensitive), discharge, crusting, masses.
  • Postnasal space (posterior rhinoscopy/flexible nasendoscopy in clinic), oral cavity/oropharynx, neck nodes; smell test (if indicated).

los.text: Describe how to diagnose and manage patients presenting with acute and chronic rhinosinusits. Nasal obstruction.
los.html:
Acute rhinosinusitis
  • Inflammation of nose and sinuses <12 weeks
  • Usually viral (common cold), secondary bacterial (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis) in ~0.5–2%.
  • Diagnosis (EPOS/NICE): nasal blockage/congestion or discharge (anterior/postnasal) plus facial pain/pressure or ↓ smell; clinical, no imaging needed.
  • Management: most resolve in 2–3 weeks: analgesia, saline irrigation, decongestants (short-term ≤7 days: rebound rhinitis medicamentosa). If >10 days: high-dose nasal corticosteroid spray (mometasone) for 14 days; back-up antibiotic (phenoxymethylpenicillin; doxycycline/clarithromycin if allergic) if systemically very unwell or worsening ("double sickening").
  • Red flags (urgent referral): periorbital oedema/erythema, displaced globe, diplopia, ↓ vision, ophthalmoplegia; severe frontal headache, frontal swelling (Pott's puffy tumour: frontal osteomyelitis), signs of meningitis, focal neurology, ↓ consciousness → CT, IV antibiotics, ENT/neurosurgery.
Chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS)
  • Symptoms >12 weeks; with nasal polyps (bilateral; ↓ smell; asthma; aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (Samter's triad)) or without polyps.
  • Ix: nasendoscopy, CT sinuses (if surgery planned or diagnosis unclear), allergy testing.
  • Mx: saline irrigation + intranasal steroid (drops for polyps), short course oral steroids for polyps, long-term macrolides (selected), functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS), biologics (dupilumab) for severe CRSwNP.
  • Unilateral polyp/symptoms, bleeding, crusting → exclude tumour (inverted papilloma, sinonasal malignancy).
Nasal obstruction causes
  • Mucosal (allergic/non-allergic rhinitis, rhinitis medicamentosa, CRS, polyps)
  • Structural (deviated septum, turbinate hypertrophy, adenoids (children), choanal atresia (neonates), nasal valve collapse)
  • Neoplastic (sinonasal tumours, nasopharyngeal carcinoma)
  • Foreign body (children)
  • Granulomatous (GPA, sarcoidosis).
  • Mx: treat cause: intranasal steroids/antihistamines (allergic rhinitis), stop decongestants, septoplasty, turbinate reduction, adenoidectomy.

los.text: Describe how to diagnose and manage patients presenting with head and neck malignancies.
los.html:
EpidemiologyMostly squamous cell carcinoma (~90%) of oral cavity, oropharynx, larynx, hypopharynx, nasopharynx, sinonasal; also thyroid, salivary gland, lymphoma.
Risk factors
  • Smoking and alcohol (synergistic)
  • HPV-16 (oropharyngeal SCC: tonsils, base of tongue; younger, non-smokers, better prognosis; p16 positive)
  • Betel nut/paan (oral cavity)
  • EBV (nasopharyngeal: Southern Chinese)
  • Occupational (wood dust: sinonasal adenocarcinoma)
  • Poor dentition
  • Immunosuppression.
Presentation (red flags: NICE 2WW)
  • Persistent hoarseness >3 weeks (≥45: laryngeal cancer).
  • Unexplained neck lump (≥45 or persistent), mouth ulcer >3 weeks, red/white patches (erythroplakia/leukoplakia).
  • Persistent sore throat/odynophagia, dysphagia, unilateral otalgia with normal ear (referred), unilateral nasal obstruction/bloody discharge, stridor, weight loss, cranial nerve palsies, trismus.
Diagnosis
  • Full ENT exam + flexible nasendoscopy
  • USS neck ± FNA/core biopsy of nodes
  • Examination under anaesthesia with biopsy (panendoscopy)
  • Staging CT/MRI neck and CT chest, PET-CT (unknown primary)
  • HPV/p16 status
  • Dental assessment.
Management (MDT)
  • by site/stage: surgery (transoral laser/robotic surgery, resection + neck dissection, laryngectomy (tracheostoma)), radiotherapy ± concurrent chemotherapy (cisplatin) (organ preservation), immunotherapy (pembrolizumab) for recurrent/metastatic
  • Supportive care: SALT (swallowing/speech), dietitian (PEG/RIG during RT), dental care (osteoradionecrosis), psychological support, smoking/alcohol cessation, surveillance (5 years).
  • Side effects of RT: mucositis, xerostomia, dysphagia, hypothyroidism, fibrosis.

los.text: Describe how to diagnose and manage patients presenting with urgent and emergency ENT conditions.
los.html:
EmergencyRecognitionImmediate management
Airway obstruction/stridor (epiglottitis, angioedema, foreign body, laryngeal tumour, deep neck space infection, haematoma after thyroid surgery)Stridor, drooling, tripod position, hoarse voice, ↑ work of breathing, ↓ sats
  • Don't examine throat in suspected epiglottitis (children)
  • O₂, nebulised adrenaline, IV dexamethasone, heliox
  • Senior anaesthetist + ENT: secure airway (intubation, surgical airway/tracheostomy)
  • Post-thyroidectomy haematoma: open wound (SCOOP)
Epistaxis (severe/posterior)Persistent bleeding, haemodynamic compromiseABC, first aid, IV access, bloods (FBC, clotting, G&S), cautery/packing, reverse anticoagulation, TXA, ENT (ligation/embolisation)
Quinsy (peritonsillar abscess)Severe unilateral sore throat, trismus, uvula deviated away, "hot potato" voice, droolingNeedle aspiration/incision and drainage, IV antibiotics (benzylpenicillin + metronidazole), steroids, analgesia, fluids
Deep neck space infections (parapharyngeal, retropharyngeal, Ludwig's angina: submandibular, dental source)Neck swelling, fever, dysphagia, airway compromiseCT, IV antibiotics, surgical drainage, airway protection
Acute mastoiditisPost-auricular swelling/erythema, protruding pinna, fever after AOMIV antibiotics, CT, ± mastoidectomy
Sudden sensorineural hearing lossHearing loss over <72 hUrgent ENT (24 h), oral steroids, audiogram, MRI IAM
Facial nerve palsyAcute LMN facial weaknessExclude ear causes (Ramsay Hunt, cholesteatoma, AOM), parotid tumour; Bell's: prednisolone within 72 h + eye protection
Foreign bodies: button batteries (nose/ear/oesophagus), food bolus obstruction (can't swallow saliva → urgent OGD), aspirated FBUrgent removal
Septal haematomaPost-trauma nasal obstruction, boggy septal swellingUrgent incision and drainage (prevent necrosis/saddle nose/abscess)
Orbital complications of sinusitis, auricular haematoma (drain), fractured nose (review at 5–7 days; reduce within 2–3 weeks)
Post-tonsillectomy haemorrhageBleeding day 0 (primary) or 5–10 (secondary: infection)Resuscitate, adrenaline-soaked swabs, H₂O₂ gargle, IV antibiotics, theatre

los.text: To link understanding of the methods of systematic review with the requirements of the literature review assignment.
los.html:
Systematic review (SR)
  • a review of a clearly formulated question that uses systematic and explicit methods to identify, select and critically appraise all relevant research and synthesise the results
  • Meta-analysis = statistical pooling of results.
Methods (and how they map to a literature review assignment)
1Clear focused question (PICO/PICOS; or PEO/SPIDER for qualitative).
2Protocol registered in advance (PROSPERO): objectives, eligibility criteria, outcomes.
3. Comprehensive search
  • Multiple databases (MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, Cochrane CENTRAL, PsycINFO), grey literature, trial registries, reference lists
  • Search strategy with keywords + MeSH, Boolean operators, truncation
  • No language restrictions ideally (limit publication bias).
4Study selection by two independent reviewers against inclusion/exclusion criteria (title/abstract → full text); PRISMA flow diagram.
5Data extraction (standardised form).
6Quality/risk-of-bias assessment (Cochrane RoB 2, ROBINS-I, CASP, Newcastle–Ottawa).
7. Synthesis
  • Narrative and/or meta-analysis (forest plot: individual study estimates with CIs, pooled diamond; heterogeneity (I²; fixed vs random effects); funnel plot for publication bias)
  • GRADE certainty of evidence.
8. DiscussionLimitations, implications for practice/research.
Literature review assignment
  • Same principles as an SR, on a smaller scale:
  • Focused question; transparent, reproducible search; explicit inclusion criteria.
  • Critical appraisal of each study; structured synthesis; acknowledge limitations.
HierarchySR/MA of RCTs at top of evidence pyramid, but only as good as included studies ("garbage in, garbage out").

los.text: Demonstrate a systematic examination of the ear, nose, and throat, identifying normal and abnormal findings
los.html:
Ear
  • Inspect pinna (deformity, scars (post-auricular: previous surgery), skin lesions, discharge), mastoid, pre-auricular sinus
  • Palpate (tragus tenderness: otitis externa; mastoid tenderness; lymph nodes)
  • Otoscopy (LO 12)
  • Hearing (whisper test, Rinne and Weber)
  • Balance tests if needed (Romberg, Unterberger, head impulse, Dix–Hallpike)
  • Facial nerve function.
NoseSee 208 LO 6 (external inspection, palpation, airway patency, anterior rhinoscopy for septum, turbinates, polyps).
Throat (oral cavity/oropharynx)
  • Good light, tongue depressor, gloves
  • Lips
  • Buccal mucosa
  • Gums
  • Teeth
  • Tongue (dorsum, lateral borders, undersurface: ulcers, leukoplakia)
  • Floor of mouth (palpate bimanually: submandibular duct/stones)
  • Hard and soft palate
  • Uvula (deviation)
  • Tonsils (size grading 1–4, exudate, asymmetry: lymphoma/SCC)
  • Posterior pharyngeal wall
  • Flexible nasendoscopy for nasopharynx, larynx (vocal cords) and hypopharynx (specialist).
NeckFrom behind; lymph node levels I–VI, thyroid (swallow/tongue protrusion), salivary glands, masses (site, size, consistency, mobility, pulsatility, transillumination).
Cranial nerves (V, VII, IX, X, XII) as relevant.
Normal vs abnormal findings
  • e.g. normal pearly-grey TM with cone of light vs red bulging TM (AOM)
  • Pink turbinates vs pale polyps
  • Symmetrical tonsils vs unilateral enlarged tonsil (lymphoma).

los.text: Perform otoscopy safely, using appropriate technique and infection control measures, while ensuring patient comfort
los.html:
Preparation
  • Explain, consent, ask about pain/discharge/surgery, check equipment (light working, disposable specula: largest that fits comfortably), hand hygiene
  • Examine better ear first.
Technique
  • Hold otoscope like a pen (same hand as the ear being examined: right ear → right hand), rest little finger/ulnar border on patient's cheek (bracing: protects if patient moves).
  • Straighten the canal: adults: pull pinna upwards and backwards; infants/young children: pull backwards (and down).
  • Insert speculum gently under direct vision into the outer (cartilaginous) canal only; avoid touching the sensitive bony canal.
  • Inspect canal (wax, debris, inflammation, foreign body, exostoses) then tympanic membrane systematically: colour, translucency, light reflex, handle of malleus, pars flaccida (attic: cholesteatoma) and pars tensa (perforation, retraction, effusion, tympanosclerosis, grommets).
  • Pneumatic otoscopy (TM mobility) if trained.
Infection controlSingle-use specula (or properly disinfected), clean otoscope, hand hygiene before/after, PPE if discharge, examine unaffected ear first to avoid cross-contamination.
ComfortStop if pain, explain throughout, children on parent's lap (hold head gently).

los.text: Recognise and interpret normal and common abnormal otoscopic findings to inform clinical reasoning
los.html:
FindingAppearanceInterpretation
Normal TMPearly grey, translucent, cone of light (anteroinferior), handle and lateral process of malleus visibleHealthy
Acute otitis mediaRed, bulging TM, loss of landmarks/light reflex, ± perforation with pusBacterial/viral AOM
Otitis media with effusionDull, retracted TM, fluid level or bubbles, amber/blue tint, ↓ mobilityGlue ear: hearing loss
PerforationHole in pars tensa (central: safer; marginal/attic: cholesteatoma risk)Post-AOM, trauma
CholesteatomaWhite keratin debris/pearly mass in attic (pars flaccida) retraction pocket, foul dischargeNeeds surgery (erodes ossicles, facial nerve, labyrinth, intracranial)
TympanosclerosisWhite chalky plaques on TMOld inflammation; usually harmless
GrommetSmall tube in TMVentilation tube (OME)
Otitis externaRed, swollen canal, debris/discharge, pain on moving tragus/pinnaTopical drops ± wick
OtomycosisFungal hyphae/spores (black/white "wet newspaper" debris)Aural toilet, antifungal drops
Wax impaction, foreign body, exostoses (bony swellings), haemotympanum (blue/red behind TM after head injury: basal skull fracture)
  • Clinical reasoning: combine with symptoms (pain, fever, hearing loss, discharge) and tuning fork tests (conductive loss with effusion/perforation/wax).

los.text: Elicit a clinical history from a patient with hearing impairment, adapting communication methods appropriately to gather relevant information about a cough
los.html:
Before
  • Ask preferred communication method (lip-reading, British Sign Language (BSL), written, hearing aid, loop system, cochlear implant)
  • Book a registered BSL interpreter if needed (not family)
  • Quiet well-lit room
  • Face the patient
  • Remove mask (or clear mask)
  • Reduce background noise.
During
  • Get attention before speaking
  • Face patient
  • Speak clearly at normal pace
  • Don't shout or exaggerate lip movements
  • Rephrase rather than repeat
  • Short sentences
  • Check understanding (teach-back)
  • Use written notes/diagrams
  • Speech-to-text apps
  • with interpreter: speak to patient, allow time.
History of a cough
  • Onset and duration (acute <3 weeks; subacute 3–8; chronic >8 weeks), character (dry/productive), sputum (colour, volume, blood: haemoptysis), timing (nocturnal: asthma/GORD/HF), triggers (exercise, cold, lying flat, eating), breathlessness, wheeze, chest pain, fever, night sweats, weight loss, hoarseness, postnasal drip, heartburn.
  • Red flags: haemoptysis, weight loss, smoker >40, persistent >3 weeks (CXR), breathlessness, chest pain, hoarseness.
  • Drugs: ACE inhibitors (dry cough), β-blockers; smoking/vaping (pack-years), occupational/environmental exposures, pets, travel/TB contacts.
  • PMH (asthma, COPD, HF, GORD), FH, social, ICE.
Common causes of chronic coughAsthma, GORD, upper airway cough syndrome (rhinosinusitis), ACEi, COPD, bronchiectasis, lung cancer, ILD, TB, HF, pertussis.

los.text: Identify and explain common communication challenges encountered with patients with hearing impairment and describe appropriate strategies to overcome them
los.html:
Common challenges
  • Patient may miss or mishear information (especially numbers, drug names, instructions)
  • Masks
  • Background noise
  • Poor lighting
  • Speaking while looking away/writing on computer
  • Talking too fast
  • Groups/multiple speakers
  • Telephone/video appointments
  • Being called from waiting rooms by voice
  • Pretending to understand (nodding)
  • Fatigue from lip-reading (only ~30–40% of speech is visible on lips)
  • Assumptions that all deaf people can lip-read or read English fluently (BSL is a separate language; written English may be a second language)
  • Interpreters not booked
  • Emergency settings.
Strategies
  • Ask and record communication needs in notes (alert flag); Accessible Information Standard (Wales: All Wales Standards for Accessible Communication).
  • Book BSL interpreters/lipspeakers/speech-to-text reporters; video relay services.
  • Environment: quiet, well-lit, face patient, hearing loop, visual call systems in waiting rooms.
  • Speak clearly, normal rhythm, plain language, rephrase, use gestures, write key points, provide written/visual information, check understanding (teach-back).
  • Allow extra time; use text/email/SMS for appointments; make sure hearing aids are working/batteries.
  • Deaf awareness training for staff; involve Deaf community organisations.

los.text: Describe and discuss barriers to healthcare access for people with hearing impairment and explain the potential consequences on health outcomes and equity
los.html:
Barriers to healthcare access
  • Communication: lack of interpreters/deaf awareness, inaccessible booking systems (telephone-only), audio announcements in waiting rooms, NHS 111/999 access (text relay/999 BSL), health information not in BSL.
  • Health literacy: lower average reading age in Deaf BSL users; fewer opportunities for incidental health learning.
  • Attitudinal: assumptions, impatience, being spoken to via companions, stigma.
  • Practical: cost/time of interpreters, short appointments, poor continuity.
Consequences on health outcomes
  • Misdiagnosis, medication errors, invalid consent, missed safety-netting.
  • Lower uptake of screening and preventive care, late presentation.
  • Worse health: Deaf BSL users have higher rates of undiagnosed hypertension, CVD risk, poor mental health and less access to psychological therapies (SignHealth studies).
  • Untreated age-related hearing loss associated with social isolation, depression, dementia (largest modifiable risk factor in Lancet Commission), falls.
Equity
  • Legal duties under the Equality Act 2010 (reasonable adjustments) and Accessible Information Standards
  • Inequity contrary to NHS principles
  • Proportionate universalism
  • Involve Deaf people in service design.

los.text: Identify accurate sources of information to confirm a patient’s drug history.
los.html:
Sources to confirm drug history(use at least two)
  • The patient (and their own list, medication packets/boxes, inhalers, injections, dosette boxes/blister packs).
  • Carers/family.
  • GP records: Welsh GP Record (WGPR) via the Clinical Portal / Summary Care Record (England), GP surgery repeat prescription list, GP letters.
  • Community pharmacy records (dispensing history, compliance aids).
  • Hospital records: previous discharge letters, clinic letters (specialist-only drugs: e.g. methotrexate, biologics, clozapine, DOACs started in clinic), medicines charts.
  • Care home MAR charts.
  • Specialist services (renal, HIV, mental health, drug and alcohol services for methadone/buprenorphine: confirm dose and last dose with dispensing pharmacy).
IncludePrescribed, OTC, herbal/supplements, recreational drugs, contraception, recently stopped drugs, allergies and reaction type, adherence, how they actually take them.

los.text: Accurately compile a list of a patient’s medications using the appropriate sources, identifying any discrepancies.
los.html:
Medicines reconciliation(NICE NG5)Obtain → verify → document an accurate list within 24 h of admission (pharmacy).
Process
  • Compile a "best possible medication history": drug name (generic), formulation, dose, route, frequency, indication, start date, last dose taken
  • Cross-check sources
  • Record source(s) used.
Identify discrepanciesOmissions, additions, wrong dose/frequency/formulation, duplications (brand and generic), drugs stopped by another clinician, intentional vs unintentional discrepancies (document reason for intentional changes).
High-risk drugs to verify carefully
  • Insulin
  • Anticoagulants (warfarin dose/INR, DOAC)
  • Antiepileptics
  • Parkinson's medicines (time-critical: give on time)
  • Opioids
  • Immunosuppressants
  • Methotrexate (weekly)
  • Lithium
  • Steroids (don't stop abruptly)
  • Antipsychotics (clozapine: checks needed if missed >48 h).
Document on drug chart (prescribe what is needed) and notes; communicate changes to patient and GP (discharge letter).

los.text: Evaluate the patient’s medications to identify any that could contribute to the cause of admission to hospital.
los.html:
• Common drug-related admissions (~5–10% of admissions): adverse drug reactions, interactions, adherence problems, inappropriate prescribing.
PresentationPossible drug causes
Falls, syncope, postural hypotensionAntihypertensives, diuretics, α-blockers, nitrates, sedatives/hypnotics, opioids, antidepressants, antipsychotics, anticholinergics, hypoglycaemics
GI bleedNSAIDs, aspirin, anticoagulants, SSRIs, steroids (with NSAID)
AKINSAIDs, ACEi/ARB, diuretics, metformin (accumulates), gentamicin, contrast, trimethoprim (↑ creatinine/K⁺)
Hyperkalaemia / hyponatraemiaACEi, ARB, spironolactone, trimethoprim / thiazides, SSRIs, carbamazepine, PPIs
HypoglycaemiaInsulin, sulfonylureas (especially with AKI)
Bleeding/over-anticoagulationWarfarin + interacting drugs (antibiotics, amiodarone), DOAC in renal impairment
Confusion/deliriumAnticholinergics (oxybutynin, amitriptyline), opioids, benzodiazepines, steroids, antiparkinsonian drugs, lithium/digoxin toxicity
Constipation/urinary retentionOpioids, anticholinergics
Bradycardia/heart blockβ-blockers, rate-limiting CCBs, digoxin, donepezil
C. difficileBroad-spectrum antibiotics, PPIs
  • Approach: STOPP/START criteria (elderly), check levels (digoxin, lithium, phenytoin), interactions, recent changes, adherence
    • Yellow Card reporting
    • stop/withhold culprit drugs ("sick day rules").

los.text: Identify any additional medications that may need prescribing for patients who are admitted to hospital.
los.html:
On admission, consider adding
  • VTE prophylaxis (LMWH, e.g. enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily) after risk assessment (bleeding vs thrombosis; renal adjustment; mechanical stockings/IPC if contraindicated).
  • Analgesia (regular + PRN; WHO ladder), antiemetics, laxatives (especially with opioids).
  • IV fluids if unable to drink, electrolyte replacement.
  • Oxygen (prescribed with target saturations).
  • Gastroprotection (PPI) if high GI risk (NSAID/steroid/antiplatelet combos, ITU stress ulcer prophylaxis).
  • Thiamine (Pabrinex) for alcohol misuse/malnutrition; alcohol withdrawal regimen (chlordiazepoxide) if dependent.
  • Nicotine replacement therapy.
  • Insulin/sliding scale (variable-rate IV insulin) for diabetic patients NBM or unwell.
  • Steroid cover (IV hydrocortisone) for those on long-term steroids when acutely unwell/NBM.
  • Time-critical medicines (Parkinson's: ensure on time, alternatives (rotigotine patch) if NBM).
  • Antibiotics for infection (per guideline), regular inhalers/nebulisers.
  • Bone protection, vaccinations (outpatient).
AlsoHold medicines contributing to admission; adjust for renal/hepatic function; document allergies.

los.text: Identify the parts of the external ear.
los.html:
Auricle (pinna)
  • Elastic cartilage covered with skin (except lobule: fat, no cartilage).
  • Parts: helix (outer rim), antihelix (inner curved ridge with superior and inferior crura), triangular fossa (between crura), scaphoid fossa (between helix and antihelix), concha (deep hollow leading to meatus: cymba above, cavum below), tragus (projection anterior to meatus), antitragus, intertragic notch, lobule.
External acoustic meatus~2.5 cm, S-shaped; lateral ⅓ cartilaginous (hairs, ceruminous and sebaceous glands), medial ⅔ bony; ends at tympanic membrane.
Innervation
  • Great auricular nerve (C2/3: posterior and lower auricle)
  • Lesser occipital (C2)
  • Auriculotemporal (V3) (anterior auricle, anterior meatus)
  • Vagus (auricular branch, Arnold's nerve) (posterior meatus/concha: cough reflex on ear syringing; referred otalgia)
  • Facial nerve (small area of concha; vesicles in Ramsay Hunt).
BloodPosterior auricular and superficial temporal arteries; lymph to parotid, mastoid, superficial cervical nodes.
ClinicalAuricular haematoma (cartilage relies on perichondrium for blood supply → necrosis/"cauliflower ear" if not drained), perichondritis (Pseudomonas, after piercing), skin cancers (BCC/SCC on helix).

los.text: Recognise the parts of the external, middle (tympanic cavity) and internal ear (i.e. including the external auditory meatus, tympanic membrane, semicircular canals, vestibulocochlear and facial nerves, malleus, incus, stapes, tensor tympani muscle, stapedius muscle and the internal carotid artery).
los.html:
External earAuricle, external auditory meatus, lateral surface of tympanic membrane.
Tympanic membrane
  • ~1 cm, oval, angled
  • Pars tensa (most; 3 layers: outer skin, middle fibrous, inner mucosa) and pars flaccida (small superior part above lateral process of malleus, lacks fibrous layer)
  • Umbo (tip of malleus handle), cone of light anteroinferiorly.
Middle ear (tympanic cavity)
  • Air-filled space in temporal bone
  • Boundaries: lateral = TM
  • Medial = promontory (basal turn of cochlea), oval window (stapes footplate), round window, prominence of lateral semicircular canal and facial canal
  • Roof = tegmen tympani (thin bone separating from middle cranial fossa)
  • Floor = jugular bulb
  • Anterior = internal carotid artery and Eustachian (auditory) tube opening, canal for tensor tympani
  • Posterior = aditus to mastoid antrum, pyramid (stapedius).
  • Ossicles: malleus (attached to TM) → incus → stapes (footplate in oval window).
  • Muscles: tensor tympani (V3; dampens malleus) and stapedius (VII; dampens stapes: hyperacusis in facial palsy).
  • Nerves: chorda tympani crossing TM medially between malleus and incus; tympanic plexus on promontory.
Inner ear (bony labyrinth in petrous temporal bone, containing membranous labyrinth with endolymph)Cochlea (2¾ turns; organ of Corti on basilar membrane; hearing), vestibule (utricle, saccule: linear acceleration), semicircular canals (anterior/superior, posterior, lateral: rotational acceleration).
Internal acoustic meatusTransmits CN VII (facial), CN VIII (vestibulocochlear: cochlear + superior/inferior vestibular nerves) and labyrinthine artery.

los.text: Locate the chorda tympani nerve and describe its path and functions.
los.html:
Chorda tympaniBranch of the facial nerve (VII) given off in the facial canal just above the stylomastoid foramen (in the mastoid segment).
Path
  • Enters middle ear through posterior wall
  • → runs forward across the medial surface of the tympanic membrane (pars tensa, near the pars flaccida), between the malleus and incus
  • → exits via the petrotympanic fissure
  • → infratemporal fossa
  • → joins the lingual nerve (V3).
Functions
  • Special sensory: taste from anterior ⅔ of tongue (cell bodies in geniculate ganglion → nucleus of solitary tract).
  • Parasympathetic (secretomotor): preganglionic fibres from superior salivatory nucleus → submandibular ganglion → submandibular and sublingual glands.
Clinical
  • Damage in middle ear surgery/otitis media → altered taste on that side
  • Facial nerve lesions proximal to chorda tympani branch affect taste (helps localise: e.g. Bell's palsy affecting taste = lesion within facial canal above chorda).

los.text: Locate the tympanic plexus.
los.html:
Tympanic plexusa nerve plexus lying on the promontory of the medial wall of the middle ear (over the basal turn of the cochlea).
Formed byTympanic nerve (Jacobson's nerve) from the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) (enters via the tympanic canaliculus from the inferior ganglion of IX) + sympathetic fibres (caroticotympanic nerves from internal carotid plexus).
Functions
  • Sensory to the mucosa of the middle ear, mastoid air cells and Eustachian tube (explains referred otalgia from the throat/tonsils via IX, e.g. after tonsillectomy, pharyngeal cancer).
  • Gives rise to the lesser petrosal nerve (preganglionic parasympathetic) → foramen ovale → otic ganglion → auriculotemporal nerve → parotid gland secretion.
ClinicalGlomus tympanicum tumour (paraganglioma) arises here (pulsatile tinnitus, red mass behind TM); tympanic neurectomy for Frey's/drooling.

los.text: Describe the anatomy of the auditory tube.
los.html:
Auditory (pharyngotympanic/Eustachian) tubeConnects middle ear (anterior wall) with the nasopharynx (lateral wall, behind the inferior turbinate; opening surrounded by the torus tubarius, with the pharyngeal recess (fossa of Rosenmüller) behind it).
Length ~3.5–4 cm in adults; runs downwards, forwards and medially (~45° in adults).
PartsLateral ⅓ bony (in temporal bone; always open), medial ⅔ cartilaginous (closed at rest), meeting at the narrowest point (isthmus).
LiningRespiratory (ciliated columnar) epithelium with goblet cells → mucociliary clearance towards nasopharynx; adenoid and tubal tonsil nearby.
Opening musclesTensor veli palatini (main; V3), levator veli palatini (X), salpingopharyngeus; opens during swallowing and yawning.
FunctionsEqualises middle ear pressure with atmosphere, drains middle ear secretions, protects middle ear from nasopharyngeal sounds/secretions/reflux.
Clinical
  • Dysfunction → negative middle ear pressure → retraction, OME, AOM, cholesteatoma
  • Barotrauma (flying, diving), patulous tube (autophony; weight loss), nasopharyngeal carcinoma in fossa of Rosenmüller → unilateral OME in an adult (red flag: nasendoscopy).

los.text: Describe the development of the paranasal sinuses.
los.html:
• Paranasal sinuses develop as outgrowths (evaginations) of the nasal cavity mucosa into surrounding bones
    • most growth is postnatal, enlarging through childhood and puberty, reaching adult size in late teens.
SinusDevelopment
MaxillaryFirst to form (~3rd–4th month in utero); present at birth (small); grows with eruption of teeth; adult size ~adolescence
EthmoidalPresent at birth (several small air cells); enlarge in childhood (hence ethmoiditis → orbital cellulitis in young children)
SphenoidalPresent as small cavity at birth; pneumatisation from ~3 yrs, mainly after 7; adult size by puberty/teens
Frontal
  • Absent at birth
  • Develops from anterior ethmoidal cells (~age 5–7), visible on X-ray ~7–8 yrs
  • Adult size after puberty
  • Often asymmetrical or absent (~5%)
  • Clinical: sinusitis patterns by age (ethmoid/maxillary in young children; frontal sinusitis and its complications (Pott's puffy tumour, intracranial abscess) in adolescents)
    • radiology interpretation in children
    • sinuses contribute to facial growth and shape changes at puberty.

los.text: Describe how the auditory tube changes with age and what effect this has on function.
los.html:
Infants/children
  • Eustachian tube is shorter (~1.8 cm at birth), wider and more horizontal (~10°), with less rigid cartilage and less effective tensor veli palatini action
  • Adenoids near the opening.
Effects in childhood
  • Poorer ventilation and drainage of middle ear
  • Easier reflux of nasopharyngeal secretions/bacteria into middle ear (especially lying flat while feeding)
  • More URTIs
  • Adenoid hypertrophy → AOM and OME (glue ear) are very common (peak 2–5 yrs)
  • Higher risk in cleft palate (abnormal tensor veli palatini) and Down syndrome.
With growth (by ~7 yrs)
  • Tube lengthens (~3.5 cm), becomes steeper (~45°) and narrower with firmer cartilage and better muscle function → middle ear disease decreases
  • Adenoids regress.
ElderlyPossible ↓ cartilage elasticity/muscle function → Eustachian tube dysfunction; patulous tube with weight loss.

los.text: Locate the lamina papyracea and the ethmoid sinuses.
los.html:
Ethmoid sinuses (air cells)
  • Multiple (3–18) thin-walled cells in the ethmoidal labyrinth, lying between the upper nasal cavity (medially) and the orbit (laterally)
  • Groups: anterior, middle, posterior (see drainage in week 207).
Lamina papyracea("paper-thin plate")
  • The orbital plate of the ethmoid bone forming the medial wall of the orbit (together with lacrimal bone, frontal process of maxilla, body of sphenoid).
  • Separates ethmoid air cells from the orbit.
Clinical
  • Very thin and may have dehiscences → ethmoid sinusitis spreads to the orbit → periorbital (preseptal) and orbital (postseptal) cellulitis, subperiosteal abscess (especially children) → proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, ↓ vision → urgent CT, IV antibiotics, drainage.
  • Medial orbital wall blowout fracture (with or without floor fracture), orbital emphysema after nose blowing.
  • Endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS) risk: breach → orbital haematoma, medial rectus injury, diplopia.
  • Anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries pass through foramina at the junction of the lamina papyracea and orbital roof (frontoethmoidal suture) → bleeding risk; landmark in surgery.

los.text: Identify the stylomastoid foramen and note how the mastoid process protects the facial nerve.
los.html:
Stylomastoid foramenInferior surface of the temporal bone, between the styloid process (anteromedial) and mastoid process (posterolateral).
TransmitsFacial nerve (VII) leaving the skull, with the stylomastoid artery.
AdultsInfants/young children
Mastoid processProjects downwards (develops in first 2 years, pulled by SCM)Absent/poorly developed
Facial nerve exitDeep and medial, shieldedSuperficial, just behind the ear
RiskProtectedForceps delivery injury, post-auricular incisions
  • Clinical: parotid surgery identifies the facial nerve trunk near the stylomastoid foramen (landmarks: tragal pointer, posterior belly of digastric, tympanomastoid suture).

los.text: Identify the three main segments (intracranial, infratemporal and extratemporal) of the facial nerve.
los.html:
Intracranial segment
  • From the pontomedullary junction (motor nucleus in pons; nervus intermedius carries taste/parasympathetic/sensory)
  • → crosses cerebellopontine angle with CN VIII
  • → enters the internal acoustic meatus.
Intratemporal segment(within the petrous temporal bone, the "infratemporal" part in the LO; in the facial (fallopian) canal)
  • Meatal (in IAM) → labyrinthine (narrowest: vulnerable to swelling in Bell's) → geniculate ganglion (first genu; gives greater petrosal nerve) → tympanic (horizontal, along medial wall of middle ear above oval window; may be dehiscent) → second genu → mastoid (vertical; gives nerve to stapedius and chorda tympani) → exits stylomastoid foramen.
Extratemporal (extracranial) segment
  • After the stylomastoid foramen: posterior auricular nerve (occipitofrontalis, auricular muscles), branches to posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid
  • → enters parotid gland
  • → divides at the pes anserinus into 5 terminal branches (temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, cervical).
Localisation by deficits
  • Lesion proximal to geniculate → loss of tearing (greater petrosal), hyperacusis, taste loss, facial weakness
  • Between geniculate and chorda → hyperacusis + taste loss + weakness (no lacrimation loss)
  • Distal to stylomastoid foramen → weakness only (parotid tumour, trauma).

los.text: Identify the branches of the facial nerve and describe their functions.
los.html:
BranchFunction
Greater petrosal nerve (geniculate ganglion)Parasympathetic → pterygopalatine ganglion → lacrimal gland, nasal/palatal glands
Nerve to stapediusDampens stapes → protects against loud sound (loss → hyperacusis)
Chorda tympaniTaste anterior ⅔ tongue; parasympathetic to submandibular and sublingual glands
Posterior auricular nerveOccipitofrontalis (occipital belly), auricular muscles
Nerve to posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoidMotor
TemporalFrontalis, upper orbicularis oculi (raise eyebrows)
ZygomaticOrbicularis oculi (close eyes)
BuccalBuccinator, orbicularis oris, upper lip muscles (cheek puffing, smile)
Marginal mandibularDepressors of lower lip and angle of mouth (depressor anguli oris), mentalis
CervicalPlatysma
  • Also a small sensory component: part of external ear (concha, behind auricle).
  • Mnemonic: "To Zanzibar By Motor Car" (Temporal, Zygomatic, Buccal, Marginal mandibular, Cervical).

los.text: Identify sites of potential accidental and surgical trauma to the facial nerve.
los.html:
Accidental trauma
  • Temporal bone fractures (especially transverse (perpendicular to petrous axis) → ~50% facial palsy; longitudinal ~20%), penetrating injuries/lacerations of face/parotid region, forceps delivery (neonates: superficial nerve, no mastoid).
  • Facial lacerations over cheek: branches (buccal, zygomatic) → explore and repair if medial to lateral canthus.
Surgical (iatrogenic) trauma
  • Middle ear/mastoid surgery (mastoidectomy, cholesteatoma surgery, stapedectomy): tympanic segment often dehiscent; mastoid segment.
  • Vestibular schwannoma surgery (cerebellopontine angle/IAM).
  • Parotidectomy (main trunk and branches) → use nerve monitoring.
  • Submandibular gland excision / neck dissection / facial surgery → marginal mandibular branch (runs along lower border of mandible: lip asymmetry).
  • Facelift/temporal surgery → temporal (frontal) branch (crosses zygomatic arch superficially: brow ptosis).
  • TMJ surgery, cosmetic procedures, local anaesthetic blocks (transient).

los.text: Identify sites where disease may affect the facial nerve.
los.html:
Intracranial
  • Stroke (UMN: forehead spared)
  • Tumours (vestibular schwannoma, meningioma at CPA)
  • MS
  • Pontine lesions (with VI palsy: Millard–Gubler)
  • Lyme disease
  • Sarcoidosis (bilateral facial palsy)
  • Guillain–Barré (bilateral)
  • HIV
  • Meningitis/basal skull infection.
Intratemporal
CauseFeaturesTreatment
Bell's palsy (commonest)Idiopathic, probably HSV-1; swelling in the narrow labyrinthine segment; onset <72 h; ~85% recoverPrednisolone within 72 h, eye care
Ramsay Hunt syndromeVZV in geniculate ganglion: painful vesicles in ear/palate, facial palsy, ± hearing loss/vertigo; worse prognosisAciclovir + steroids
Ear diseaseAcute otitis media (dehiscent canal), cholesteatoma, necrotising otitis externa, mastoiditisTreat cause
OtherTemporal bone fracture, glomus tumours, facial nerve schwannoma
ExtracranialParotid malignancy (facial palsy + parotid mass = malignant until proven otherwise), parotid surgery/trauma, facial lacerations.
SystemicDiabetes, pregnancy (↑ Bell's), Melkersson–Rosenthal syndrome, leukaemia infiltration.
AlwaysExclude UMN cause, examine ears (otoscopy), parotid, other cranial nerves; protect the eye (lubricants, tape at night: corneal exposure).

los.text: Relate form to function of the outer, middle and inner ear.
los.html:
Outer ear (collection)
  • Auricle funnels sound and helps sound localisation (vertical and front–back: spectral cues from folds)
  • External acoustic meatus acts as a resonator (~2.5 cm tube amplifies frequencies ~2–5 kHz, speech range), protects TM (S-shape, hairs, cerumen: lubrication, antimicrobial, traps debris; self-cleaning epithelial migration).
Middle ear (impedance matching/amplification)
  • Transfers airborne sound to fluid-filled cochlea (otherwise ~99.9% reflected): area ratio of TM to oval window (~17:1) + ossicular lever (~1.3:1) → ~20–25× pressure gain (~25–30 dB).
  • Acoustic reflex (stapedius, tensor tympani) dampens loud sounds.
  • Eustachian tube equalises pressure.
  • Conductive hearing loss when this fails.
Inner ear (transduction)
  • Cochlea: stapes footplate vibrates oval window → travelling wave along basilar membrane (base: stiff/narrow → high frequencies; apex: wide/floppy → low frequencies: tonotopy) → hair cells in organ of Corti (inner hair cells: main sensory; outer hair cells: amplify via electromotility (prestin)) bend stereocilia against tectorial membrane → K⁺-rich endolymph enters → depolarisation → glutamate → spiral ganglion → cochlear nerve. Round window allows fluid movement. Damage to basal turn first in noise/ageing (high-frequency loss).
  • Vestibular apparatus: detects head position and movement → balance (LO 35).

los.text: Describe how the anatomy and functions of the macula and ampulla differ and what they detect.
los.html:
Macula (utricle and saccule: otolith organs)Ampulla (crista ampullaris of semicircular canals)
LocationUtricle: horizontal macula; saccule: vertical maculaDilated end (ampulla) of each of the 3 semicircular canals
StructureHair cells with stereocilia/kinocilium embedded in a gelatinous otolithic membrane topped by otoconia (calcium carbonate crystals)Hair cells embedded in a gelatinous cupula (no otoconia), which spans the ampulla like a swing door
DetectsLinear acceleration and static head tilt (gravity): utricle → horizontal movement (car accelerating); saccule → vertical (lift)Angular (rotational) acceleration of the head in the plane of each canal (3 orthogonal canals: lateral/horizontal, anterior/superior, posterior)
MechanismGravity/inertia shifts heavy otolithic membrane → bends hair cellsEndolymph lags behind head rotation (inertia) → deflects cupula → bends hair cells; adapts with sustained rotation
Hair cell physiology
  • Bending towards kinocilium → depolarisation (↑ firing)
  • Away → hyperpolarisation (↓ firing)
  • Tonic baseline firing allows bidirectional signalling
  • Paired canals work in push–pull.
Clinical
  • BPPV = displaced otoconia from the utricle into a semicircular canal (usually posterior)
  • → makes canal gravity-sensitive
  • → brief vertigo with position change.

los.text: Describe the vestibulo-ocular reflex.
los.html:
Vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR)Stabilises gaze during head movement by producing eye movements equal and opposite to head movements (latency ~10 ms) → keeps image on the fovea.
Pathway (horizontal VOR, head turns right)
  • Right lateral semicircular canal excited (left inhibited)
  • → vestibular nerve
  • → vestibular nuclei (medulla/pons)
  • → contralateral abducens nucleus (VI)
  • → left lateral rectus, and via medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF)
  • → ipsilateral oculomotor nucleus (III)
  • → right medial rectus
  • → both eyes move left (opposite to head).
  • Three-neuron arc
  • Cerebellum (flocculus) calibrates gain.
Clinical tests
  • Head impulse (thrust) test: rapid small head turn while fixating; corrective saccade = peripheral vestibular loss on that side (e.g. vestibular neuritis); normal in central causes (part of HINTS).
  • Doll's eye (oculocephalic) reflex in comatose patients (intact brainstem: eyes move opposite to head); caloric testing (cold water → nystagmus fast phase away ("COWS": Cold Opposite, Warm Same)) for brainstem death testing (absent).
NystagmusImbalance of vestibular input → slow drift of eyes towards the weaker side + fast corrective phase away from it (peripheral: unidirectional horizontal, suppressed by fixation).
DysfunctionOscillopsia (visual world bounces with movement: bilateral vestibular loss from gentamicin toxicity).
